planting.note: Direct sow in fall where chaparral or coastal-sage conditions mimic its native range; resents summer irrigation once established and will rot in heavy clay held wet through summer.

directions: A chaparral and coastal-sage perennial that blooms heavily in late spring with deep purple-to-blue flowers and white-centered upper petals on branched spikes, this larkspur goes summer-dormant, making it a good fit for dry-summer native gardens that need a disappearing vertical accent. Give it excellent drainage and let foliage die back naturally after bloom — this dormancy is normal, not plant failure. Pairs well with California poppy and golden yarrow in a dry perennial border that gets winter-spring water only.

planting.note: Scatter seed on open, grassy ground in October-November and let winter rains do the germinating; avoid any summer supplemental water.

directions: A California endemic with some of the most saturated blue-purple flowers in the genus on compact stems, this larkspur's striking color and open grassland habit make it an excellent centerpiece for spring wildflower meadows and bulb or annual mixes. Treat as a fall-sown wildflower-meadow component rather than a border perennial, since it dies back to a dormant rootstock each summer and avoiding summer water is the single most important factor for success. Stick to the mainland straight species rather than the rare Channel Island subspecies, which are unsuitable for general trade.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall under oak or foothill-woodland canopy for dappled light and leaf-litter mulch; full sun in hot inland gardens will scorch it.

directions: A shorter, shade-tolerant woodland larkspur with dark blue reflexed sepals, this species gives gardeners a native alternative to cultivated dwarf delphiniums for the understory and part-shade niche where most delphinium cultivars struggle. It goes dormant and vanishes by early summer, so interplant with later-emerging ferns or sedges to avoid bare patches. This fills a genuinely distinct niche from the taller, sun-loving California larkspurs already common in cultivation.

subcategory: Great Basin xeric rock garden perennial

planting.note: Direct-sow with cold stratification into lean, fast-draining sandy or gravelly soil; rich garden soil or regular irrigation will kill it via root rot.

directions: A true desert and Great Basin larkspur with brilliant dark-blue sepals and white upper petals, this species' drought and cold tolerance make it the best candidate in the genus for xeric, high-desert rock-garden plantings rather than moist perennial borders. It goes fully dormant by midsummer, so site it where that gap is expected, among other Great Basin xerophytes. It hybridizes naturally with related species where ranges overlap, so keep seed sources isolated if species purity matters.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall for natural outdoor stratification into consistently moist soil along a pond edge, streambank, or low meadow spot; expect to stake or shelter from wind due to its very tall spikes.

directions: A dramatic back-of-border perennial reaching three to six feet with stout pale-green stems and dense blue-purple racemes, this larkspur fills the niche of a giant moisture-loving native across a huge Alaska-to-Arizona range, distinct from the already-present woodland and chaparral species. Unlike the summer-dry chaparral larkspurs, it comes from riverbank and subalpine-meadow habitat and will not tolerate drought. Division in spring or early autumn is a reliable way to bulk up stock faster than seed.

planting.note: Direct-sow with cold-moist stratification into consistently damp montane meadow, seep, or streambank soil; site away from livestock, since foliage and seed are significantly toxic.

directions: A robust Rocky Mountain montane-meadow perennial tolerant of both full sun and light shade, this larkspur is useful for naturalistic meadow or streamside plantings in colder interior-West gardens where the California coastal species aren't hardy. This needs consistently damp soil — montane meadow, seep, or streambank conditions — and will underperform in a standard dry perennial bed. Give it room; at full size it rivals the largest mountain larkspurs and works best as a background plant behind lower meadow perennials.
sources: US Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)

planting.note: Fall-sow outdoors and let seed stratify naturally over winter; reserve for cold-climate gardens with a genuine subalpine wet meadow or aspen-grove microclimate.

directions: One of the showiest and longest-lived North American wildflowers, documented living 75 or more years, this larkspur forms four-to-seven-foot stands of inky-blue to deep-purple racemes that dominate Rocky Mountain subalpine meadows. Because it is extremely long-lived once established, treat it as a permanent structural planting rather than a border perennial to be divided or moved. As with other tall mountain larkspurs, this species is acutely toxic to livestock and should be sited away from pastured animals.
